More than five centuries ago, when da Gama set sail for India, his ability to foresee danger was limited. Midway through the voyage, his sailors’ limbs and gums began to swell and bleed; many grew weak and died without warning. But spare a thought for the world’s official timekeepers, who’ll be gathering on the outskirts of Paris in mid-October to vote on a proposal to drop the “leap second” – the adjustment we use to keep clocks aligned with Earth’s rotation. Official time uses ultra-precise atomic clocks, and the definition of a second is based on the decay of Caesium-133. But Earth’s day-night shift, or solar time, depends on how fast the planet spins. The pace of this rotation – and the length of any given day – varies depending on the moon’s gravitational pull on the planet, geophysical processes in Earth’s core and shifts in its mass. The exact number at which this happens varies from region to region, but using Purdue’s global average and adjusting for local purchasing power and inflation, Remitly has worked out the figure for each of the UK’s major cities. When two new branches of frozen yoghurt store Yomi opened within a month of each other, queues were out the doors. Other brands popping up all over Auckland – and social media feeds – seem hugely popular. Why, after a decade, is froyo back in fashion? Teal colourways are back on shelves. Skinny jeans are being spotted on the streets. Frozen yoghurt shops are everywhere. You could almost think Auckland was back in 2014. Right at the centre of it all is Yomi. Beginning as a standalone shop in Mount Maunganui in December 2025, Yomi is a reimagined frozen yoghurt store. Think KiwiYo but on an entirely different level. The first thing to notice is that the toppings are seemingly endless. Chocolate and lollies. Strawberries and passionfruit. Chia pudding or Biscoff cheesecake – both house-made. With many of Yomi’s ingredients organic and sourced locally, it can cater to even the most diet-focused patrons. items.article: In a new book, German artist and writer Philipp Ruch argues that viewing the ascent of Hitler’s NSDAP through the prism of the Third Reich has distorted our understanding of fascism’s electoral breakthrough With your art collective Centre for Political Beauty you famously built a replica of the Holocaust memorial on a property next to the home of an AfD politician . Now you’ve written a history book about the Nazis’ rise to power. Don’t we already know everything there is to know about the 1932 elections, the Reichstag fire and the Enabling Act of 1933? About three years ago I became interested in how Hitler’s National Socialist German Workers’ party (NSDAP) rose to prominence when Germany was still a democracy, because I hoped it could tell us something about the success of rightwing extremist movements today. From looking at historical sources, I realised that the Reichstag elections of 14 September 1930 were in many ways more important than what happened in 1932 and 1933. And I expected it to be an open-and-shut case. But the more I looked into it, the more I realised that most of the theories we have to explain the rise of the Nazis don’t make sense – the data tells a completely different, far darker story. Why were the 1930 elections so important? The numbers behind the vote were astonishing. In 1928, the NSDAP got 800,000 votes and 12 seats in the Reichstag. items.article: Ever wondered what happened to Jumanji child star Bradley Pierce? Find out all about his life after finding fame in the 90s… Bradley Pierce is remembered by many as Peter Shepherd in the hit 1995 family adventure film Jumanji , in which two children stumble across an ancient board game that opens the door to a magical jungle world. The child actor starred opposite Robin Williams, Bonnie Hunt and Kirsten Dunst in the iconic fantasy film, which has since expanded into a billion-dollar franchise complete with multiple sequels and a theme park ride. Bradley, now 43, landed a string of major roles as a youngster in the 1990s – voicing Chip in Disney's Beauty and the Beast , playing a young Andrew Donovan in Days of Our Lives , voicing Tails in the Sonic the Hedgehog f ranchise, and starring as Dylan Moody in the sitcom Shaky Ground. But have you ever wondered what Bradley is up to now? Find out all we know about his life 30 years later... Following his breakout role in Jumanji, Bradley lent his voice to a number of hit TV series and films throughout the 90s and early noughties, including The Pink Panther, The Little Mermaid, and High School Musical 3: Senior Year. Bradley also played Peter Lender in the fantasy film The Borrowers and Ricky James in the rom-com, Down to You , starring Freddie Prinze Jr. and Julia Stiles.
